title: Bookmaker-exchange inter-market arbitrage (soccer)
mechanism: Betting exchanges (Betfair-style; structurally the same as Kalshi/Polymarket/Novig/ProphetX order books) let a crowd of traders post back/lay prices independently of any single bookmaker's risk book, so the exchange-implied probability and a given bookmaker's quoted price periodically diverge enough that a bet at the bookmaker plus the opposite lay at the exchange locks a guaranteed return; many bookmakers 'position-take' (reprice infrequently) rather than continuously rebalance to the exchange, so the gap is not closed instantly.
claimed_edge: Franck, Verbeek and Nuesch (2013, Economica 80(318):300-325, 'Inter-Market Arbitrage in Betting') find that combining a bet at a bookmaker with the opposite position at a betting exchange yields a guaranteed positive return in 19.2% of matches across the top five European soccer leagues, and report bookmakers posting negative-margin (arbitrageable) combined prices against the exchange with some regularity, not just as rare outliers.
data_needed: Simultaneous, timestamped bookmaker odds and betting-exchange back/lay prices for the same match/market (soccer 1X2); no current lab dataset carries any exchange-side price.
skeptic_note: Data are from the mid-2000s to 2011, before exchanges and bookmakers both got faster/more automated; opportunity frequency and size have likely shrunk since, and 19.2% counts ANY guaranteed-positive combined position, not necessarily one large enough to clear commission/transaction costs at real stake size.

title: Account/position-limit management suppresses realizable cross-book arbitrage
mechanism: Bookmakers that behave as 'position-takers' (infrequent odds changes) actively detect and restrict bettors who look informed or arbitrage-seeking, instead of continuously repricing to match the wider market the way 'book-balancer' bookmakers do; so even where a cross-book price discrepancy mathematically exists, the leg at the position-taking book is often unavailable at the needed stake because that account gets limited or the bet gets rejected, which keeps many on-paper arbitrage opportunities from ever being realized.
claimed_edge: Grant, Oikonomidis, Bruce and Johnson (2018, European Journal of Finance 24(18):1799-1816, 'New entry, strategic diversity and efficiency in soccer betting markets: the creation and suppression of arbitrage opportunities') identify 545 cross-bookmaker arbitrage portfolios in their sample and find that around 50% of them require betting the favourite specifically at a 'position-taking' bookmaker, the type of bookmaker they show actively restricts informed bettors -- i.e. account management, not pricing, is the binding constraint on realizing roughly half of the identified opportunities.
data_needed: Per-bookmaker classification (position-taker vs book-balancer), account-level limiting/restriction history, and matched cross-book prices at the stake size actually sought, for the same match/market and time window.
skeptic_note: This directly undercuts naive 'X% of games have an arbitrage' as a usable edge estimate -- the realizable fraction is roughly half the nominal count once account management is factored in. The paper is UK/European-soccer-specific; mapping to US books/exchanges (which have their own, less-studied limiting practices) is an analogy, not a tested transfer.

title: US sportsbooks explicitly cite arbitrage-pattern detection when limiting accounts
mechanism: US sportsbook risk teams monitor for betting patterns correlated with known arbitrage or bonus-abuse networks (e.g. stake sizing mirrored against a specific set of counter-books, or behavior matching previously flagged accounts) and cap maximum stake well below normal recreational limits once flagged, which caps the realizable size of any individual arbitrage or middle regardless of the nominal price gap found.
claimed_edge: Reporting on Massachusetts' new bettor-limiting disclosure requirement (Legal Sports Report, 2025) quotes operator-stated reasons for limiting that explicitly name arbitrage: DraftKings cited activity 'indicative of targeting perceived market inefficiency,' and Fanatics cited 'a network of restricted users that signal potential arbitrage positions.' The same reporting states 73% of unrestricted active accounts were lifetime losers vs 52% of restricted accounts, and 25% of unrestricted accounts were net winners vs 48% of restricted accounts.
data_needed: Account-level stake-limit history matched to bet-level CLV/arbitrage-flag data from inside a sportsbook's own risk system -- operator-internal data that no public dataset provides.
skeptic_note: These are self-reported operator rationales disclosed under new MA regulatory pressure, not an independently audited sample; the 73%/52%/25%/48% figures describe winners generally (likely mostly skilled handicappers, not specifically arbitrageurs), so treating them as if they measured arbitrage bettors specifically overstates what was shown.

title: US peer-to-peer exchanges (ProphetX, Novig) structurally remove the winner-limiting incentive
mechanism: ProphetX and Novig are peer-to-peer order-book exchanges that match bettor-to-bettor and earn a commission on net winnings rather than taking the other side of every bet, so -- unlike a traditional sportsbook, where a consistently winning account is a direct liability to the house -- they have no risk-book incentive to limit that account. This removes the enforcement mechanism described in the account-limiting entries above, but only to the extent the exchange has enough resting liquidity on the other side of the trade to actually fill the bet at size.
claimed_edge: Practitioner reviews (LegalSportsReport's ProphetX vs Novig comparison, OddsShopper's 'How Does Novig Work', PropsBot) describe both platforms' commission-on-net-winnings model (roughly up to ~2% on ProphetX net winnings, 0% on ProphetX parlays/losing bets; Novig described as 0% commission on many pre-game straight trades) as removing the structural reason to limit winners; LegalSportsReport states plainly that 'ProphetX doesn't limit winning accounts... because Prophet doesn't hold positions, they have no reason to limit winning accounts.'
data_needed: Documented, independently verified account-level history on ProphetX/Novig showing large, consistently winning accounts retained at full stake size over a long period, compared against a matched traditional-sportsbook limiting curve; nothing like this was found published anywhere.
skeptic_note: These are practitioner/marketing-adjacent reviews, not independent audits or regulatory data. Even if the no-limiting claim holds, the practical constraint shifts from account limits to resting order-book depth: thin liquidity means a large arbitrage/middle stake simply cannot be filled at the quoted price, which caps realizable size by a different mechanism rather than proving a sustainable, scalable edge.

title: Cross-platform prediction-market arbitrage (Kalshi vs Polymarket), sports a top category by count
mechanism: Kalshi and Polymarket price the same real-world events (including sports outcomes) independently via separate order books driven by each platform's own user base and liquidity rather than a shared bookmaker risk system, so the same underlying event can trade at different implied probabilities on the two venues at the same time; buying the cheaper side on each platform (e.g. YES on one, NO on the other) locks a profit whenever the combined cost of both legs is below $1 after fees.
claimed_edge: An August 2025 arXiv preprint by IMDEA Networks researchers ('Unravelling the Probabilistic Forest: Arbitrage in Prediction Markets', arXiv:2508.03474, not yet peer-reviewed) analyzed roughly 86 million bets across thousands of prediction markets from April 2024 to April 2025 and found about $40 million in identified cross-platform arbitrage profit; sports markets showed more arbitrage opportunities BY COUNT than any other category including politics, though the typical sports opportunity was reported as smaller in size than politics-market opportunities. The top 3 wallets alone placed over 10,200 bets and profited $4.2 million, consistent with automated/bot execution.
data_needed: Simultaneous, timestamped Kalshi and Polymarket order-book snapshots (best bid/ask, not just last trade) for the same sports contract, matched at second-level granularity, plus each platform's fee schedule at the time.
skeptic_note: Not peer-reviewed (preprint only, direct arXiv access was blocked from this environment so this is based on press coverage of the paper, not a direct read of its tables). Reported profits are concentrated in bot-like, high-frequency wallets; a retail bettor without automation likely captures little to none of this, and 'more opportunities by count' could just reflect the sheer number of sports contracts listed rather than larger or more persistent per-contract mispricing.

title: Surebet count rose across bookmakers as betting exchanges grew, even as average overround fell
mechanism: As Betfair-style exchanges grew market share and offered close-to-true-probability pricing (margin limited to commission), competing fixed-odds bookmakers were pushed to cut their own margins to stay competitive; this combination of thinner average margins plus an independent exchange price to compare against increased the count of identifiable surebets among bookmakers even while the market-wide average margin (overround) was shrinking.
claimed_edge: Gomez-Gonzalez and Del Corral (2018, Economics and Business Letters 7(4):129-136, 'The betting market over time: overround and surebets in European football') studied major bookmakers across Europe's top five leagues from the 2000-01 through 2016-17 seasons and report (per secondary summaries of the paper) a continuous decline in average overround alongside an increase in the number of surebets identified among major bookmakers in more recent seasons, a trend attributed to the growth of betting exchanges such as Betfair.
data_needed: A long panel (15+ years) of closing odds from the same set of major bookmakers plus exchange prices, by season, to replicate the overround/surebet time trend and check whether it continued into the 2020s as US books and prediction markets entered.
skeptic_note: Direct full-text access to this paper (uniovi.es, dialnet.unirioja.es) was blocked from this research environment, so the specific percentage figures could not be independently confirmed here -- this entry relies on search-result abstracts describing the paper's conclusions, not a direct read of its tables; a backtest agent or human should pull the primary source before relying on exact numbers.

title: Middling two books' differing point-spread/total numbers (claimed long-run positive EV)
mechanism: Different bookmakers move the same spread or total line at different speeds and to different final numbers in response to injury news, weather, or sharp action; betting the same side against two books' differing numbers (e.g. -2.5 at book A, +3.5 at book B) wins BOTH bets if the final result lands in the narrow 'middle' window between the two numbers, and otherwise only costs the vig on the single losing leg, so the strategy is claimed to be profitable long-run provided the probability-weighted value of occasional double-wins exceeds the vig drag from the far more common single-win/single-loss outcome.
claimed_edge: Multiple independent practitioner guides (BettingUSA, Action Network, Las Vegas Advisor, SportsBettingDime) describe this mechanism consistently. One specific numeric claim found: a 'basketball 2-point middle laying no more than -110 on each side is profitable over the long term for both sides and totals' -- but none of these sources published a backtested win rate, sample size, or realized ROI to support that specific number.
data_needed: Paired, timestamped point-spread/total lines from at least two distinct US sportsbooks for the same game (not just one book's closing line), plus the final margin/total, to compute how often the result lands inside a given middle window and whether win-rate-times-payout clears the vig cost on the no-middle outcomes.
skeptic_note: No peer-reviewed study or even a real, numbered backtest/track record was found for middling specifically -- every source is a how-to guide, not a results page. None of the current lab datasets carry two different books' lines for the same game, so this cannot be tested without new data; this is exactly the 'sounds right, never shown' pattern the standing orders warn to grade down, hence 'claim' rather than 'practitioner_data'.

title: Best-of-book MLB strikeout prop pricing already shows sub-100% combined implied probability in ~2-3% of closing snapshots
mechanism: Sportsbooks price a player's strikeout over/under independently of each other and do not communicate; when a bettor takes the single best available price for 'over' at whichever book posts it and the best available price for 'under' at whichever (possibly different) book posts it, the two best prices occasionally come from books that disagree enough about the pitcher's expected strikeouts (or lag the market on one side) that the combined implied probability falls to or below 100%, a mechanical dutch-book/arbitrage condition rather than a directional edge.
claimed_edge: This is a direct measurement against the lab's own lab/devdata/mlb_k_props.parquet (5,340 rows), not an external study: over_book differs from under_book in 84.0% of rows (confirming the stored over/under prices are genuinely best-of-multiple-books, not one book's own two-sided price); the mean combined implied probability (over_odds_american + under_odds_american converted to probability) is 103.9% (an average ~3.9% synthetic hold); in 2.06% of rows the combined implied probability is strictly below 100%, and in 2.92% it is at-or-below 100%. The general practice this measures -- shopping multiple books for player props because props are priced less efficiently than game lines -- is widely described by practitioners (e.g. line-shopping guides) but no external source was found quoting this specific incidence rate for MLB strikeout props.
data_needed: Already present in mlb_k_props: over_odds_american, under_odds_american, over_book, under_book. A stronger test needs confirmation that the two best-of-book prices were available SIMULTANEOUSLY to a real bettor (the schema does not expose a timestamp per book-side, only one snapshot time for the row), since the dataset is described as a ~4h-before-first-pitch best-of-books snapshot.
skeptic_note: A 2-3% incidence of sub-100% combined price in the historical closing-ish snapshot is a real base rate in this dataset, but it is not automatically a tradeable arbitrage: (1) the snapshot likely already picks the single best price per side without recording whether both prices were live at the same instant, so leg/execution risk is not captured; (2) 2-3% of rows times whatever edge exists when it happens could still be thin after realistic bet sizing, book limits, and slippage; (3) this is one pre-game snapshot, so it says nothing about how often such windows open and close intraday, which is the actually tradeable frequency.

title: Stake-not-returned free bets have a formally optimal hedge probability, confirmed on tennis odds
mechanism: Sportsbook promotional free bets are almost always structured as 'stake not returned' (you keep only the winnings, not the stake) specifically because a stake-returned free bet on a short-odds favorite would let a customer convert it to near risk-free cash; this stake-not-returned structure means the guaranteed value from hedging (betting the free bet then laying it off, matched-betting style) is a nonlinear function of the bet's win probability, and is maximized at a specific probability rather than at the shortest odds available, which determines which markets/selections a promo should be hedged on to extract maximum value.
claimed_edge: Karl Whelan (University College Dublin), 'The Economics of Free Bets' (dated March 30, 2026, working paper on the author's site), derives that under a simple constant-margin bookmaker pricing rule keeping fraction m of money staked on average, the guaranteed hedged value of a stake-not-returned free bet is maximized when the bet's win probability equals sqrt(m*(1-m)), and reports that empirical odds on tennis bets are consistent with this prediction.
data_needed: Promo/free-bet terms (stake-not-returned vs stake-returned, minimum odds requirements) matched to the odds and bookmaker margin at the moment the free bet is placed, plus an exchange or second-book price to hedge against; no current lab dataset carries promotional-offer data at all.
skeptic_note: Direct full-text access to karlwhelan.com was blocked from this research environment, so this summary relies on search-result snippets describing the paper's model and conclusion, not a direct read of its proofs or tennis dataset; separately, practitioner sources describe matched-betting/free-bet profitability as declining sharply in 2025-2026 as bookmakers both shrink free-bet sizes and restrict accounts that repeatedly claim and hedge them, which this paper's theoretical optimum does not address.

title: Prediction markets' lower headline margin is mostly illusory at real bet size -- order-book depth is the actual constraint
mechanism: Kalshi, Polymarket, Betfair Exchange, Novig, SX Bet and other order-book venues post their best price from a single resting limit order, which can reflect a tiny retail order rather than deep market-making; a low displayed margin at the top of the book says nothing about how much can be filled at that price, so the apparent low-hold/arbitrage edge versus a traditional sportsbook's always-large-size -110 line often cannot be captured for a stake that matters, which is the real-world execution-risk limit on this whole topic's thesis (closer to a sportsbook's account-limit problem than people assume: it's venue illiquidity, not venue restriction).
claimed_edge: A dataset comparison across 7 venues (Kalshi, Polymarket, Betfair Exchange, Novig, SX Bet, Duel, and sportsbooks) on 2026 NFL Week 1 moneylines found Polymarket.us quoting a margin of about 0.49% to 0.98% on different fixtures -- roughly six times tighter than Pinnacle's margin -- but with only $0.00 to $7.22 of stake capacity available at that best price on the thinnest fixtures, while Kalshi, priced third-tightest, had $751 to $3,901 of depth on the same fixtures, a roughly 100x-to-500x depth advantage despite a worse headline price.
data_needed: Full order-book depth (not just best bid/ask) at multiple size tiers, timestamped, across sportsbooks and exchanges for the same game/market, to compute the realistic size-weighted average price a bettor could actually achieve rather than the headline top-of-book number.
skeptic_note: This is a single-week, single-sport snapshot from a practitioner/industry blog, not a systematic multi-season study, so it is unclear how representative these specific depth numbers are generally; it does, however, directly contradict any registry entry (this topic's S001/S005/S006 above) that cites a low headline margin or 'X% of games have an arbitrage' without also checking fillable size, and should be read as a standing caveat on all of them.
